questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
questions.solution:
'Half of the world's languages are expected to ___' — the passage is about language death: **vanish**. Flourish, multiply and return reverse or ignore the gloomy forecast.

**Answer: vanish**
questions.passage: Half of the world's seven thousand languages are expected to (1) ___ by the end of this century. When a language dies, a community loses more than words: songs, jokes and remedies that took centuries to (2) ___ disappear with it. Digital tools offer some hope. Recordings and online dictionaries can (3) ___ the sounds of a language long after its last speaker has gone. Yet preservation is not the same as life. A language survives only when children (4) ___ to learn it at home, and that choice depends on prestige and jobs, not on archives. Successful revivals therefore begin in schools and markets, where the language is once again (5) ___ daily.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
questions.solution:
'Songs, jokes and remedies that took centuries to ___' — culture accumulates slowly: **evolve**. Purchase and imitate do not fit 'took centuries'; evaporate clashes with the idea of things worth keeping.

**Answer: evolve**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution:
Recordings and dictionaries can ___ the sounds of a language: keep them safe for later listeners — **capture**. Discard and mute destroy; distort corrupts the sound instead of saving it.

**Answer: capture**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
questions.solution:
'That choice depends on prestige and jobs' — the blank must set up the word 'choice': children **choose** to learn the language at home. Refuse, fail and pretend contradict the survival the sentence describes.

**Answer: choose**
questions.shortcut: The next sentence repeats 'choice' — echo it.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
questions.solution:
'Schools and markets, where the language is once again ___ daily' — living use in real places: **spoken**. Archived, recorded and translated all keep the language behind glass, which the passage has just rejected as 'not the same as life'.

**Answer: spoken**
questions.shortcut: Markets + schools = mouth, not machine.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Building more roads is the only lasting cure for congestion.
Economists should replace engineers in city planning departments.
Congestion charging is an effective response to urban traffic, and the claim that it burdens the poor does not survive scrutiny.
Every city should ban private cars from its centre.
questions.solution:
The passage argues that free road space is wasted scarce capacity, shows charging works wherever tried, and then dismantles the 'tax on the poor' objection. A repeats the failed old remedy; B exaggerates a single contrast; C is a ban, never proposed in the text.

**Answer: Congestion charging is an effective response to urban traffic, and the claim that it burdens the poor does not survive scrutiny.**
questions.shortcut: Thesis = pricing works + the objection fails.
questions.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, cities treated congestion as an engineering problem: when a road filled up, the remedy was to build another. The remedy kept failing. Within a few years every new lane was swallowed by traffic that had waited, latent, for the space to appear, and planners learned an uncomfortable truth — capacity creates its own demand. Economists read the same streets differently. Road space at nine in the morning is a scarce good that drivers consume for free, and anything free is consumed until it is scarce. Congestion charging simply attaches a price to what was being wasted.

The results in cities that have tried the idea are difficult to dismiss. In every case — Singapore first, later London and Stockholm — traffic inside the charged zone fell by double digits within two years, buses moved faster, and a share of the revenue flowed into better public transport. The charge also performs a quieter service: it makes visible what drivers had been paying all along in time, fuel and fumes.

Critics call the charge a tax on the poor. The argument sounds powerful until it meets the data. In most cities the poorest households own no car at all and depend on the very buses that congestion charging speeds up. What the charge truly removes is the privilege of the better-off driver who expected to store a private vehicle on public streets for nothing. That expectation, not the toll, is the real subsidy — and it was never free.

questions.q: According to the passage, newly built lanes quickly fill up because —
options: traffic engineers miscalculate the width of lanes
waiting traffic appears as soon as the space exists, since capacity creates its own demand
cities deliberately encourage people to buy cars
buses occupy most of the new lanes
questions.solution:
The passage states it directly: traffic that 'had waited, latent, for the space to appear' — 'capacity creates its own demand'. A, C and D invent causes the passage never offers.

**Answer: waiting traffic appears as soon as the space exists, since capacity creates its own demand**
questions.shortcut: Quote the em-dash line: it is the stated cause.

questions.q: The author describes the free storage of private cars on public streets as 'the real subsidy' because —
options: drivers receive road space without paying its true cost, which everyone bears in time, fuel and fumes
governments transfer cash directly to car owners
parking fees are refunded by the municipality
public transport consumes more fuel than private cars
questions.solution:
A subsidy = a benefit paid by others. The passage makes the cost explicit — 'time, fuel and fumes' — and calls the toll 'what drivers had been paying all along' invisibly. B and C invent refunds; D reverses the environmental charge.

**Answer: drivers receive road space without paying its true cost, which everyone bears in time, fuel and fumes**
questions.shortcut: Subsidy = hidden cost shifted to the public.

questions.q: The word 'swallowed' as used in the passage suggests that new lanes were —
options: quickly consumed by the traffic that had been waiting
questions.solution:
'Every new lane was swallowed by traffic that had waited' — the image means the new space was **used up at once** by latent demand. Width, tolls and depth are physical readings of a figurative verb.

**Answer: quickly consumed by the traffic that had been waiting**
questions.shortcut: Swallowed by X = X took it all.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
options: Why Free Roads Are the Most Expensive Roads
A History of the Motor Car
questions.solution:
The passage's spine — free road space is consumed to scarcity, pricing fixes it, the hidden subsidy ends — is captured by **Why Free Roads Are the Most Expensive Roads**. A and D each touch one line; B mocks the very experts the passage criticises.

**Answer: Why Free Roads Are the Most Expensive Roads**
questions.shortcut: Title test: cover paragraph 1, 2 and 3 at once.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Crop diversity is vital insurance against disease and climate change, and it must be kept both in seed banks and in living fields.
Seed banks have made on-farm conservation unnecessary.
High-yielding varieties should be banned from cultivation.
The potato famine could recur only in Europe.
questions.solution:
The passage moves from the danger of genetic uniformity to vaults as backup, then insists that real conservation is living, evolving farm cultivation with vaults behind it. B reverses the final paragraph; C exceeds the text's warning; D shrinks a global argument to one historical event.

**Answer: Crop diversity is vital insurance against disease and climate change, and it must be kept both in seed banks and in living fields.**
questions.shortcut: Last paragraph = the thesis restated.
questions.passage:
Modern agriculture wears a dangerous uniformity. A few high-yielding varieties of rice, wheat and maize now feed most of humanity, and the thousands of local strains that farmers once nurtured are fading from the fields. Uniformity is profitable and perilous in equal measure: when every plant shares the same genes, a single disease or a slow shift in climate can meet no resistance anywhere. The potato famine of the nineteenth century remains the classic warning.

Seed banks are the insurance vaults of this risk. In cold rooms across the world, botanists store hundreds of thousands of samples — old farmer varieties, rare crops, and the wild relatives of domesticated plants. The wild relatives matter most. Growing unnoticed in hedgerows and hills, they carry genes for drought tolerance, heat resistance and salt endurance that breeders can transfer into cultivated crops. Because a new variety takes a decade to breed, the work must begin long before the crisis arrives.

Yet vaults, however impressive, are only half a defence. Stored seeds are frozen snapshots; crops evolve in fields, alongside pests and weathers that change every season. A variety kept alive only in a freezer stops adapting. The most durable conservation therefore happens on farms, where communities keep growing their old strains, adjusting them year by year, and hand down seed and knowledge together. Seed banks should back up this living system, not replace it. Diversity is not a museum exhibit. It is a working population of plants that must keep living — and keep changing — to remain useful.

questions.q: According to the passage, the wild relatives of crop plants are especially valuable because they —
options: produce more grain than modern varieties
need no water at any stage of growth
carry genes for drought, heat and salt tolerance that breeders can transfer into crops
are immune to every disease known to science
questions.solution:
The passage lists their gifts exactly: 'genes for drought tolerance, heat resistance and salt endurance'. A exaggerates yield; B and D overstate tolerance into absolutes the text never claims.

**Answer: carry genes for drought, heat and salt tolerance that breeders can transfer into crops**
questions.shortcut: Detail Qs: find the list, match the words.

questions.q: The author calls stored seeds 'frozen snapshots' to suggest that —
options: vaults preserve varieties exactly as farmers grew them centuries ago
seeds in vaults stop adapting to changing pests and climates, unlike crops grown in fields
photography is an essential tool of botanical research
freezers gradually alter the genes of stored samples
questions.solution:
The contrast is with crops that 'evolve in fields, alongside pests and weathers that change every season'; a variety only in a freezer 'stops adapting'. C is literal noise; D invents freezer damage; A states the metaphor's surface, not its point.

**Answer: seeds in vaults stop adapting to changing pests and climates, unlike crops grown in fields**
questions.shortcut: Snapshot = a moment fixed, while life moves on.

questions.q: The word 'perilous' as used in the passage most nearly means —
questions.solution:
'Uniformity is profitable and perilous in equal measure' sets reward against risk: perilous = **dangerous**. Profitable is the balancing word, not the meaning; orderly and modern do not fit the warning that follows.

**Answer: dangerous**
questions.shortcut: X is A and B in equal measure: B is the opposite pole of A's praise.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
options: The Story of the Potato Famine
How to Build a Seed Vault
The Living Insurance of Crop Diversity
questions.solution:
**The Living Insurance of Crop Diversity** spans all three paragraphs — the risk, the vaults, the farms. A and D cover single paragraphs; B reduces the argument to architecture.

**Answer: The Living Insurance of Crop Diversity**
questions.shortcut: The title must survive the last paragraph.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

GREGARIOUS
questions.solution:
Gregarious (Latin grex, flock) = fond of company, **sociable**. Greedy borrows the 'gre-' look; dangerous and gloomy are unrelated to the social sense.

**Answer: sociable**
questions.shortcut: greg- = flock: gatherer, not grabber.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

VOLUNTARY
questions.solution:
Voluntary = done by one's own will; its antonym is **compulsory** (forced). Willing and optional are synonyms; casual changes the register, not the compulsion.

**Answer: compulsory**
questions.shortcut: voluntary ↔ compulsory; optional ≈ voluntary.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

ABATE
questions.solution:
Abate = to lessen, grow weaker — **subside** (the storm abated). Intensify and expand are antonyms; permit is a false friend from the 'a-bate' look.

**Answer: subside**
questions.shortcut: abate → abating storm → dies down → subside.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

NOVICE
questions.solution:
A novice is a beginner; the antonym is a **veteran**, one with long experience. Beginner, learner and apprentice are all synonyms arranged as decoys.

**Answer: veteran**
questions.shortcut: novice ↔ veteran: new ↔ seasoned.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate one word for the given expression.

One who can speak many languages
questions.solution:
**Polyglot** = speaker of many languages (poly = many, glotta = tongue). Bilingual limits the number to two; a polygamist has many spouses; a calligrapher writes beautifully.

**Answer: Polyglot**
questions.shortcut: poly- (many) + glot (tongue).

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate one word for the given expression.

A remedy that cures all diseases
questions.solution:
**Panacea** (Greek pan, all + akos, remedy) is the cure for everything. An antibiotic fights bacteria only; a narcotic dulls the senses; a placebo is a dummy medicine with no healing power.

**Answer: Panacea**
questions.shortcut: pan- = all (pan-India, panorama).

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate one word for the given expression.

A person who hates mankind
questions.solution:
**Misanthrope** (misein, to hate + anthropos, mankind) hates humanity. A philanthropist loves mankind — the designed opposite; a misogynist (not misogamist, who hates marriage) hates women; an optimist merely hopes.

**Answer: Misanthrope**
questions.shortcut: mis- = hate, anthropos = man.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To pull someone's leg
options: to help someone climb a ladder
to injure someone in a fall
to tease someone by playing a joke
questions.solution:
To pull someone's leg = **to tease or joke with someone in fun**, never with real harm. The literal options translate the leg image; flattery is a different social act altogether.

**Answer: to tease someone by playing a joke**
questions.shortcut: Body-part idioms are almost never literal.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A white elephant
options: a rare animal kept in a zoo
a costly possession that is useless to its owner
a gift that brings good luck
questions.solution:
From the Siamese custom of gifting sacred white elephants whose upkeep ruined the receiver: **a costly but useless burden**. Rarity, loyalty and luck all miss the burden sense.

**Answer: a costly possession that is useless to its owner**
questions.shortcut: White elephant = expensive + useless, both needed.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To smell a rat
options: to suspect that something is wrong or deceitful
to find the kitchen in a filthy state
questions.solution:
To smell a rat = **to sense trickery or foul play** before it is proved. Filth and hunger take the rat literally; treasure invents a reward the idiom never promises.

**Answer: to suspect that something is wrong or deceitful**
questions.shortcut: Rat = sneaky business; smell = detect.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution:
**Occurrence** doubles both the c and the r, and ends -ence, not -ance: occur + rence. Occurence drops an r; occurrance trades the ending; ocurrence drops a c.

**Answer: Occurrence**
questions.shortcut: occur → occurred → occurrence: double c, double r throughout.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution:
**Connoisseur** (French) keeps the full 'nois' group — c-o-n-n-o-i-s-s-e-u-r — with double n, double s and the rare -eur ending. The others each shed or reshuffle one of these chunks.

**Answer: Connoisseur**
questions.shortcut: con + nois + seur: count the doubles, nn and ss.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

The number of applicants (a) seeking admission (b) have increased sharply this year (c) No error (d)
questions.solution:
'The number of + plural noun' is singular — The number of applicants **has** increased. ('A number of applicants have…' would take the plural.) The error sits in part (c).

**Answer: have increased sharply this year**
questions.shortcut: The number → singular; a number → plural.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

The scenery of Almora (a) are famous (b) for its pine forests (c) No error (d)
questions.solution:
'Scenery' is an uncountable noun and always singular: The scenery of Almora **is** famous. The error is in part (c).

**Answer: are famous**
questions.shortcut: scenery, furniture, luggage, information → singular.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

When I reached home (a) my mother has already (b) cooked the dinner (c) No error (d)
questions.solution:
The dinner was finished before the past act of reaching: the earlier past takes the past perfect — **had** already cooked. 'Has' (present perfect) cannot sit beside 'reached'.

**Answer: my mother has already**
questions.shortcut: Earlier of two past acts → had + V3.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

He is one of the finest orators (a) that our country (b) has ever produced (c) No error (d)
questions.solution:
In 'one of the finest orators that our country has ever produced', 'that' is the object of 'produced'; the subject of the relative clause is 'our country', which is singular, so 'has' is correct. Every part of the sentence is right.

**Answer: No error**
questions.shortcut: In 'one of the + plural … that', check whether 'that' is the subject (plural verb) or the object (verb agrees with its own subject).

questions.q:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the sentence.

My sister is more smarter than any of her classmates.
questions.solution:
'Smarter' is already comparative; 'more' doubles it. The clean fix adds an intensifier: **much smarter than**. B keeps the doubling; C keeps the error; D stacks two superlatives.

**Answer: much smarter than**
questions.shortcut: never more + -er together.

questions.q:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the sentence.

No less than fifty delegates were absent from the conference.
questions.solution:
Countable nouns take **fewer**, uncountable ones take less: fifty delegates → No fewer than fifty delegates. B also confuses than/then; C is not an idiom.

**Answer: No fewer than**
questions.shortcut: numbers you can count → fewer.

questions.q:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the sentence.

Being a rainy day, we cancelled the picnic.
options: Owing to being a rainy day
questions.solution:
The participle 'being' needs a subject, and 'we' is not a rainy day — a dangling modifier. The absolute construction **It being a rainy day** supplies the missing subject. A keeps the error; B piles words on it; C is unidiomatic.

**Answer: It being a rainy day**
questions.shortcut: Ask: who is 'being' a rainy day? Nobody — add 'It'.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The principal, along with the senior teachers, ___ attending the workshop.
questions.solution:
'Along with', 'as well as' and 'together with' never change the subject: the verb agrees with 'the principal' — singular **is**. Are, were and have been all agree with the nearer plural, the standard trap.

**Answer: is**
questions.shortcut: strip the 'along with…' phrase, then match the verb.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The auditor was accused ___ tampering with the records.
questions.solution:
Fixed collocation: **accused of** + gerund/noun (a person is charged *with* an offence, but accused *of* one). For, with and into are not the collocation.

**Answer: of**
questions.shortcut: accuse OF; charge WITH.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The gardener is watering the plants.
options: The plants are watered by the gardener.
The plants have been watered by the gardener.
The plants were being watered by the gardener.
The plants are being watered by the gardener.
questions.solution:
Present continuous → **is/are being + V3**: are being watered. A drops the continuous; B shifts to present perfect; C shifts to past continuous.

**Answer: The plants are being watered by the gardener.**
questions.shortcut: is/are + V-ing → is/are being + V3.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

Let the door be shut.
questions.solution:
A passive imperative ('Let + object + be + V3') becomes a plain order in active voice: **Shut the door.** B keeps 'let' and breaks the structure; C and D remain in or slip into the passive.

**Answer: Shut the door.**
questions.shortcut: Let + be + V3 → drop 'let', use the bare V3 as an order.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said to me, "Where do you live?"
options: He asked me where I lived.
He asked me that where I lived.
He asked me where did I live.
He asked me where do I live.
questions.solution:
Reported question: said to → **asked**, question order becomes statement order, tense backshifts: where **I lived**. B keeps the impossible 'that'; C and D retain question order and the present tense.

**Answer: He asked me where I lived.**
questions.shortcut: asked + wh-word + subject + verb (backshifted).

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The teacher said, "The earth revolves around the sun."
options: The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth had revolved around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth was revolving around the sun.
questions.solution:
A universal truth keeps its present tense even after a past reporting verb: the earth **revolves** around the sun. B backshifts wrongly; C and D distort the timelessness of the fact.

**Answer: The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.**
questions.shortcut: Universal truths never backshift.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful paragraph.

**1.** Tea is more than a beverage in India. **P:** Vendors pour it between two containers to cool it, a small performance repeated a million times a day. **Q:** It punctuates the day from dawn till midnight. **R:** The chaiwala, with his kettle and glass tumblers, is part of every street and station. **S:** Conversations over tea seal deals, settle quarrels and welcome guests. **6.** No drink is more deeply woven into daily life.
questions.solution:
**Q** extends 'more than a beverage' into the day's rhythm → **S** gives the social work tea does → **R** introduces the person who serves it → **P** zooms into the serving act itself, the closest image to S6's 'woven into daily life'. QSPR.

**Answer: QSPR**
questions.shortcut: Idea → social uses → server → serving act; P must follow R.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful paragraph.

**1.** The camel is built for the desert. **P:** Its wide, padded feet spread on hot sand instead of sinking into it. **Q:** Even its water needs are modest: it drinks hugely when water is found, then manages for days. **R:** Long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out the driving sand. **S:** Its hump stores fat, which the body slowly converts into energy when food is scarce. **6.** Every part of the animal answers some demand of the desert.
questions.solution:
**P** (feet) and **R** (eyelashes, nostrils) form the physical-defence pair → **S** (fat stored) and **Q** (water managed) form the fuel-and-water pair, with S's food leading naturally to Q's drink. PRSQ; S6 then sums up every part.

**Answer: PRSQ**
questions.shortcut: Group the parts: body parts first, fuel/water second.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful paragraph.

**1.** Paper has a remarkable history. **P:** For centuries the method travelled slowly westward, reaching Baghdad and then Europe. **Q:** The Chinese court official Cai Lun is credited with improving its making around 105 AD. **R:** Before paper, people wrote on bark, clay, silk or sheepskin, all of them costly or clumsy. **S:** Cheap paper made books affordable, and affordable books changed the world. **6.** Few inventions have democratised knowledge so completely.
questions.solution:
**R** sets the pre-paper scene → **Q** names the inventor → **P** follows the technique westward → **S** delivers the consequence, books, which S6's 'democratised knowledge' immediately echoes. RQPS.

**Answer: RQPS**
questions.shortcut: Before → invention → spread → consequence; S must sit beside S6.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to complete the paragraph.

The city's new bicycle lanes have changed more than traffic. Shopkeepers report more customers stopping on their way home. Children cycle to school in groups that grow larger every month, and the air in the central wards feels cleaner on weekdays. ___
options: Bicycles are manufactured in several Indian states.
Success, it seems, arrived not with announcements but with habits.
The mayor cycles only on weekends for exercise.
Critics want the lanes removed at the earliest.
questions.solution:
The paragraph stacks small, quiet changes, so it closes on the idea that habit, not announcement, produced them — **Success… arrived not with announcements but with habits**. Manufacturing, the mayor's weekend and angry critics all break the paragraph's direction.

**Answer: Success, it seems, arrived not with announcements but with habits.**
questions.shortcut: The closing sentence must ride the paragraph's momentum.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to complete the paragraph.

Herbaria — collections of pressed plants — look like rooms full of old folders. Yet each sheet is data: where the plant grew, when it flowered, who collected it. ___ Climate researchers now compare flowering dates across a hundred and fifty years to track a warming world.
options: Folders in herbaria are made of acid-free paper.
Pressed plants can keep their colour for many decades.
Read across decades, such sheets become a record of change.
Collectors often worked alone in remote districts.
questions.solution:
The blank must bridge 'each sheet is data' to researchers comparing dates across 150 years: **Read across decades, such sheets become a record of change.** Paper quality, colour and lonely collectors are true-ish details that lead nowhere.

**Answer: Read across decades, such sheets become a record of change.**
questions.shortcut: Bridge blank: repeat the key idea of the sentence before AND after.
